ol96b1-c13061.summary: Auriol's question whether the habit acquired by theological study is one or many, prompted by Lombard's single volume gathering many matters. Opening arguments ground theology's unity in the simplicity of habits, the light of faith, the probative middle of divine authority, the formal object (deity), the concurrence of these, or the indivisible divine object present to each part; contrary arguments deny any habit is one and say theology is several (God and creature share nothing univocal; it overlaps metaphysics and physics). Article 1 asks what a science is. Henry's indivisible intensifiable quality, Scotus's aggregate of complete partial habits, and Bernard's order of species are refuted. Science is a permanent habit determining the intellect to one simple act grasping a conclusion through its principle, distinct from remembered demonstrations, as choice reaches means through the end. Article 2: a science's numerical unity is that of a whole, the mutually perfecting connection of partial habits along and across chains of demonstration. Article 3 refutes accounts of theology's unity: Thomas's revealability, unity by revealing authority, by middle, Scotus's formal object, concurrence, and Godfrey's two habits. Article 4: specific unity comes from one mode of knowing (way of taking principles, demonstrating, and the intellect's stance), so theology, uniformly using whatever aids faith to declare the articles, is one habit numerically and specifically. Related conclusions of other sciences may be attached to it, as in mixed sciences, and God and creatures fall under it by attribution.
claims: Science is a permanent habit by which the intellect grasps a conclusion through its principle in one simple act.
A science is numerically one by the connection of its partial habits into a whole.
A science is specifically one by a single mode of knowing and proper logic.
Theology is one habit, numerically and specifically, defined by its declarative mode of using whatever supports faith.
Revealability, authority, middle, or formal object alone do not explain the unity of theology.
Theology is not two habits, practical and speculative.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e107.summary: Title of the question: whether the habit acquired by theological study is one or many.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e114.summary: Ties the question to Lombard's prologue, which speaks of the unity of his short volume gathering so many matters and Fathers' sentences, and raises whether the theological habit is one or many.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e128.summary: Rubric for arguments that theology is one habit from the general nature of any habit.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e135.summary: Argues that every form in the soul is simple and indivisible: an accident is a simple form, without matter-form parts, without quantitative parts (the soul's accidents are spiritual), and without potential parts. The theological habit is such a form, so it is one.
claims: (Argument) Every accidental form in the soul is simple and indivisible.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e161.summary: Argues a fortiori: accidents of the soul are more unified than bodily accidents, and whiteness is one simple form, so every habit of the soul, theology included, is one.
claims: (Argument) Spiritual accidents are more unified than bodily ones.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e174.summary: Argues that habits in the intellect are no less simple than those in the will, and justice is one simple virtue, so science is one simple quality and the theological habit is one.
claims: (Argument) Intellectual habits are as simple as volitional virtues.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e190.summary: Rubric and first argument that theology is one by unity of light. What gives a habit unity is that whose presence brings unity and whose absence removes it. The same object known in different lights yields different habits (the blessed in glory, we in faith's enigmatic light), and theology proceeds in all its truths, however diverse, under the one supernatural light of faith, so it is one habit.
claims: (Argument) Unity of light gives unity to a habit.
(Argument) Theology proceeds under the one light of faith.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e238.summary: Argues that a science's unity comes from the unity of its habit of principles, which is like a light (De anima III, intellect as habit like light), and theology is one through faith, which extends to everything believed about God, Christ, angels and creatures.
claims: (Argument) A science's unity comes from its habit of principles.
(Argument) Faith unifies theology.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e261.summary: Argues that things belonging to different sciences under different lights can be comprehended in one habit when referred to one light. Creator, creature and physical matters, which belong to different sciences naturally, can fall under one theological habit through faith's single supernatural light.
claims: (Argument) Referral to one light unifies diverse matters in one habit.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e285.summary: Rubric for arguments that theology is one by its middle term (medium).

ol96b1-c13061-d1e290.summary: Argues that sciences are distinguished by their terms and definitions (Metaphysics VI: mathematics abstracts from sensible matter, physics includes it), and definitions are middle terms in demonstration. So a habit's unity comes from its probative middle, and theology is one because it rests on divine authority as its probative middle.
claims: (Argument) A habit's unity comes from its probative middle.
(Argument) Divine authority is theology's single probative middle.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e319.summary: Argues that what leads the knower to the object distinguishes habits, since different leading principles yield different cognitions and habits, and the middle leads to the object. So unity and distinction come from the middle.
claims: (Argument) The middle that leads to the object distinguishes habits.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e343.summary: Argues from one knowable known through different middles: that the earth is round belongs to astronomy through the rising and setting of signs (Ptolemy) and to physics through the equal tendency of parts to the center (Aristotle). Astronomy and physics are distinguished only by their middles.
claims: (Argument) The same conclusion through different middles belongs to different sciences.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e376.summary: Rubric for arguments that theology is one by the formal character of its object.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e382.summary: Argues that a science is one if it concerns one genus of subject with its parts and properties (Posterior Analytics I). Theology has one formal object, God, considering everything insofar as it is divine, so it is one.
claims: (Argument) A science is one through one subject genus.
(Argument) Theology considers all things insofar as divine.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e402.summary: Argues that unity of habit follows the formal object as unity of power does: sight is not diversified by stars, men or stones, since it reaches all under one formal character (color or light). So theology is one by the unity of its formal object.
claims: (Argument) A power's unity comes from the unity of its formal object.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e422.summary: Argues that unity of definition and terms gives habits unity (Metaphysics VI), and the definition expresses the object's formal character, so theology is one by it.
claims: (Argument) Definition expresses the formal object and gives unity.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e438.summary: Rubric for the argument that theology is one through the concurrence of all these factors.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e443.summary: Argues that what arises from several conditions together is removed when one fails. Unity of habit is prevented by diversity of light (our science and the blessed's, both of God), of formal object (physical sciences, all under the natural light, are diverse habits), and of middle. So unity requires all three, and theology, with one light, one formal object (deity) and one probative middle (God's authority), is maximally one.
claims: (Argument) Unity of habit requires unity of light, formal object and middle together.
(Argument) Theology has all three unities.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e489.summary: Supports the concurrence view: Aristotle attributes unity of habit to the object (Posterior Analytics I) and to definition and middle (Metaphysics VI), which would not be true unless each contributed.
claims: (Argument) Aristotle attributes unity to object, definition and middle.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e506.summary: Rubric for the argument that theology is one because an indivisible object is present to each of its parts.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e515.summary: Begins the argument that theology is supremely one because of an indivisible object assisting each part indivisibly, even if it comprises three habits: science, faith, and knowledge of what is deduced. (The sentence continues in the next paragraph.)
claims: (Argument) Theology may comprise several habits unified by one indivisible object.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e528.summary: Continues, in badly corrupted text: in each part theology has God as object, supremely one and indivisibly present. Whatever has many forms can be one through one indivisible form present to all its parts, as a human with several forms is more one than a stone through the rational soul indivisibly present to every part. So theology is supremely one.
claims: (Argument) Plurality of parts can be unified by one form present indivisibly to all.
(Argument) God as object unifies theology like the soul unifies a human.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e559.summary: Supports the point from the first question: theological procedure generates opinion, faith, and a non-adhesive, declarative habit. These can combine into one theology only as all concern one object, God, so theology's unity comes from the indivisible object present to each part. (The text is partly corrupt.)
claims: (Argument) Theology's component habits are unified only by their common object.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e581.summary: Rubric for the contrary arguments: neither theology nor any habit is one.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e586.summary: Argues that what is acquired successively has part after part and is not one, and theology and every science are acquired part by part.
claims: (Argument) Successively acquired habits have parts and are not one.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e607.summary: Argues that science is just an ordered arrangement of intelligible species, not a disposition to receive species or acts, since the intellect is fully apt. One science contains many really distinct species, so it has no unity.
claims: (Argument) Science is an ordered set of intelligible species.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e631.summary: Argues that the intellect cannot be assimilated by one indivisible thing to many things of different kinds, yet science assimilates it to triangle, circle and square, all within geometry. So no science is truly one.
claims: (Argument) One indivisible form cannot assimilate the intellect to many diverse objects.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e651.summary: Rubric for arguments that theology in particular is not one habit.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e658.summary: Argues that things sharing no formal character cannot belong to one habit, and God and creature share nothing univocal, yet both belong to theology. So theology is not one.
claims: (Argument) God and creatures share nothing univocal.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e678.summary: Argues that a habit treating God and intelligences as distinctly as metaphysics, and the soul and human beings as distinctly as natural philosophy, cannot be one, or physics and metaphysics would be one habit. Theology treats God more excellently than metaphysics and the soul more exquisitely than physics, so it is not one. Confirmed: the first question showed that theological study sometimes yields a metaphysical habit, and likewise a physical one regarding soul, human being, prime matter and time. (The text is partly corrupt.)
claims: (Argument) Theology includes matters of metaphysics and physics treated distinctly.
(Argument) Theological study can yield metaphysical and physical habits.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e717.summary: Rubric marking the response to the question.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e723.summary: Lays out the response in four steps: the doctors' opinions on the unity of a scientific habit in general, Auriol's view of it, the doctors' opinions on theology's unity in particular, and Auriol's view of that.

ol96b1-c13061-Dd1e745.summary: Surveys and refutes the doctors on the unity of a scientific habit, then gives Auriol's account of what science is. Against Henry, science is not one indivisible quality intensified by degrees: knowing the first conclusion does not enable knowing the hundredth, partial habits are generated and intensified separately, and error about one conclusion coexists with knowledge of others. Against Scotus, science is not a generic aggregate of complete partial habits, one per conclusion, since these would be neither species nor mere numerical individuals and would denominate their possessor only imperfectly. Against Bernard, science is a whole but not an order of species, since a relation cannot be produced first, cannot be a principle of action, and no kind of ordering of species fits. Auriol's account: science is neither species, order, nor memory of demonstrations, but a permanent habit determining the intellect to one simple act that grasps a conclusion's truth through and together with its principle's truth, as choice reaches means through the end. Its conditions: the conclusion is known only through the principle, in a single act, which needs a determining habit, distinct from remembered demonstration (shown by sudden expert insight), and permanent.
claims: Science is not one indivisible quality intensified by degrees.
Science is not an aggregate of complete partial habits.
Science is not an order of intelligible species.
Scientific knowing is one simple act grasping the conclusion through the principle.
Science is a permanent habit distinct from remembered demonstrations.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e754.summary: Rubric naming Henry of Ghent's opinion (Quodlibet IX q. 4).

ol96b1-c13061-d1e759.summary: States and refutes Henry's view that a science covering many conclusions is one indivisible reality in the intellect, generated whole in essence by the first demonstration and merely intensified by later ones (first degree for the first conclusion, second for the second, and so on), as one indivisible power extends to many objects. Refutation: whoever has a habit can use it, but one with the first degree cannot know the hundredth conclusion, so different realities in the habit regard different conclusions. Nor do degrees help: conclusions are finite while degrees of an intensible form are potentially infinite; on Henry's own view degrees are not really distinct, yet the intellect cannot newly act without a real change; and if the habit for the hundredth conclusion were really the same as the first, one who knows the first could at once know the hundredth, contrary to experience.
claims: (Reported) A science is one indivisible habit intensified by successive demonstrations.
One who has a habit can use it, yet knowing the first conclusion does not enable knowing the hundredth.
Degrees of intensity cannot explain distinct conclusions.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e881.summary: Further refutation of Henry: habits with distinct generations, corruptions, intensifications and remissions are really distinct, not degrees of one essence. Habits of the first ten conclusions can be generated and intensified without that of the hundredth (meditating on Euclid I does not teach Euclid XV).
claims: Habits with independent generation and intensification are really distinct.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e919.summary: Further refutation of Henry: contrary habits cannot coexist, and error about the hundredth conclusion (positive ignorance) is contrary to science of it, yet it can coexist with science of the first ten. So those habits are not really one; otherwise the whole science would conflict with error about any conclusion. The paragraph then introduces Scotus's opinion (Ordinatio prologue q. 4 and 5): science has generic unity, with as many partial habits as conclusions, unified by common matter (different habits for the Physics, De caelo, and so on), supported by the contrary arguments. Auriol objects. Habits for innumerable conclusions, most still undiscovered, cannot be specifically distinct sciences. Nor can they differ only numerically, since then two habits of the same conclusion in Aristotle and Plato would differ only numerically, though they agree more than habits of different conclusions. So they are not complete partial habits.
claims: Error about one conclusion can coexist with science of others, so these habits are really distinct.
(Reported) A science has generic unity, comprising as many complete partial habits as conclusions.
Partial habits of a science are neither distinct species nor merely numerically distinct complete habits.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e1039.summary: Further objections to Scotus. If there were several complete habits, physics in the soul would be an aggregate unity like grammar, logic and mathematics together, against Aristotle's one-science-one-subject-genus. And as a form is in being, so it denominates: the habit of ten geometry conclusions denominates its possessor imperfectly (he is not a perfect geometer), so it is not a complete habit predicable like an individual or species of geometry.
claims: Physics is not a mere aggregate of complete habits.
Partial knowledge denominates its possessor only imperfectly, so it is not a complete habit.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e1087.summary: Further objection to Scotus: as conclusions relate to knowability, their habits relate to science, and conclusions are parts of one integral knowability, none being complete knowability, so their habits are not complete sciences. (The end is corrupt.)
claims: Conclusions are parts of one integral knowability.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e1103.summary: Rubric naming the opinion of Bernard (of Auvergne) in his attacks on Henry's Quodlibet IX q. 4.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e1110.summary: States Bernard's view: science is neither one indivisible form nor an aggregate of specific habits, but a whole with parts, namely an ordering of species in the intellect by which we understand readily at will. Auriol grants that science is a whole but denies it is an ordering of species. A scientific habit comes from discursive acts, and what such an act leaves is either a pure order impressed on species (impossible: a relation cannot be the first term of production), the species themselves (they existed before), or something absolute grounding the order (nothing besides species, habits and acts is in the intellect, so that would be a habit).
claims: (Reported) Science is an ordering of intelligible species.
Science has the unity of a whole.
Science cannot be a mere order of species, since a relation cannot be the first term of production.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e1178.summary: Further objections to Bernard. A scientific habit is something absolute in the category of quality, though related to act and object, while an order of species is a relation of species to each other. And science is a habit of the conclusion, but an order of species regards the whole demonstration (major extreme to middle, middle to minor).
claims: Science is an absolute quality, not a relation among species.
Science is a habit of the conclusion, not of the whole demonstration.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e1210.summary: Further objection: an order, being a relation, cannot be a principle of understanding or any operation, while science is a first act and principle of the second act of understanding the conclusion.
claims: A relation cannot be a principle of operation.
Science is a first act grounding the act of understanding.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e1223.summary: Further objection by division. The order of species would be spatial (species have no place in intellect), causal (they precede the habit and are caused by phantasm and agent intellect), formal (then it would exist as soon as species are impressed, but science does not), or one of use (then it comes not from the species but from something added that inclines the intellect to use them in order). So science is not an order.
claims: Species have no spatial, causal or formal order that constitutes science.
An ordered use of species requires a determining habit beyond the species.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e1273.summary: Rubric announcing what the scientific habit is, formally and in reality.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e1280.summary: Auriol's account of what science in the soul is. It is not the species (one with the species of 'triangle' and 'three angles' does not thereby know the theorem), not their order, and not what determines the intellect to use them in order, which is memory of the earlier discursive act. Memory is not science: remembering is reflexive (we remember having understood), while knowing bears directly on the object, and memory covers the whole syllogism while science is of the conclusion. Nor is it a readiness to demonstrate. Acts reveal habits, and the intellect has three kinds of act: a simple one bearing on a simple object (objectively simple, what is understood and that by which coincide); one bearing on a complex truth through its terms as formal reason; and one bearing on a complex truth through another complex truth. Each is really one simple intellection. Compare the will's simple volition of the end and its choice of means for the end. As the second act requires the habit of principles, the third requires a habit determining the intellect to see a conclusion's truth through the principle's truth. Science is that habit, distinct from remembered demonstration and permanent. Its conditions are proved next.
claims: Science is neither species, nor their order, nor memory of demonstration.
Memory is reflexive and covers the whole syllogism; science bears directly on the conclusion.
The intellect has three kinds of act: simple apprehension, knowing principles through terms, and knowing conclusions through principles.
Science is a permanent habit determining the intellect to one simple intellection of a conclusion through its principle.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e1428.summary: First condition: the intellect grasps a conclusion's truth only insofar as it grasps the principle's truth. As a thing is to being, so to truth and knowability, and a conclusion has being from the principle ('if the principle is, the conclusion is'). Likewise, as means have goodness only from the end and are desired only as the end is desired, so a conclusion has truth only from the principle.
claims: A conclusion's truth and knowability derive from the principle's.
The intellect reaches a conclusion only through its principle, as the will reaches means only through the end.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e1491.summary: Further proof of the first condition. If the intellect reached a conclusion's truth by itself, it would do so from the conclusion's terms (it would then be a principle), from the joining of terms (known only from the terms), or by the intellect's own weighing (the intellect is moved by objects, and even principles need the terms). So it reaches the conclusion only through the principle's truth, as knowing is knowing through a cause (Posterior Analytics I). Second condition: this intellection of both truths is one simple act. If the act reaching the conclusion did not reach the principle, it would find truth in the conclusion by itself, which it lacks, as a bitter potion is desirable only as joined to health.
claims: A conclusion cannot be known from its own terms, their joining, or the intellect's weighing.
Scientific knowing is knowing through the cause.
One simple act reaches both the conclusion and the principle.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e1588.summary: Further proof of the second condition: the act of knowing that this is because of that, or that this causes that, reaches both cause and caused at once, and scientific knowing is exactly that, not merely knowing that something is (which is understanding a principle).
claims: Scientific knowing grasps cause and effect in one act.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e1614.summary: Further proof by analogy: knowing is to the intellect what choosing is to the will, as understanding principles is to willing the end, and one simple act of choice reaches the means because of the end. The end's goodness is the formal reason of the means' goodness, and the principle's being is the formal reason of the conclusion's, with the conclusion known materially; material and formal objects do not multiply acts. This holds for every science, not only propter quid, since in all scientific knowing the principle is known as cause of the conclusion's truth (being as copula, 'third adjacent'). Third condition: something in the intellect determines it to this act, since it can err about conclusions and needs determination to act rightly.
claims: Scientific knowing is to intellect as choice is to will.
Material and formal objects do not multiply acts.
In every science the principle is known as cause of the conclusion's truth.
The intellect needs a determining habit for acts in which it can err.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e1692.summary: Further proof of the third condition: as the will needs something determining it to right choice, so the intellect needs something for scientific knowing. Fourth condition: this determinant is other than remembered demonstration. Demonstration compels the act at the end of a deduction (hence 'apodictic syllogism', making one know), but the act leaves a habit, since every act generates a conforming habit (one becomes a harpist by playing).
claims: Demonstration determines the intellect at the end of the deduction.
Repeated acts generate conforming habits.
The scientific habit is distinct from the memory of demonstrations.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e1753.summary: Further proof of the fourth condition: the will, though freer than intellect, is sometimes moved to choose suddenly, without counsel, from habits, and virtue appears most in sudden acts (Aristotle). So the intellect is sometimes determined to its act by habit rather than syllogistic discourse.
claims: Habits produce sudden acts without deliberation.
The intellect can know conclusions by habit without actual demonstration.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e1779.summary: Further proof from experience: those trained in a science sometimes see a conclusion's truth shining from the principle without syllogizing, as skilled artisans act without deliberating ('art does not deliberate'), which would not happen if they were always determined by remembered demonstration. Fifth condition: the habit is immanent and permanent ('hard to move', Categories). This completes the account of the scientific habit.
claims: Experts see conclusions in principles without discursive reasoning.
Science is an immanent, permanent habit, hard to remove.

ol96b1-c13061-Dd1e1826.summary: Auriol's view on the numerical unity of a scientific habit, in three propositions. A science is one by totality, not simplicity, continuity or aggregation. 'Science' loosely means the memory of a science's demonstrations, which has the unity of an ordered whole like a syllogism; properly it means the habit of knowing conclusions through principles. Science properly is one total habit whose form is the mutual, perfecting connection of partial habits, lengthwise through chains of conclusions and widthwise through shared middles. This formal unity explains successive acquisition, the coexistence of partial knowledge and partial error, and the expert's sound judgment of new cases.
claims: A science has the unity of a whole.
Retained demonstrations are science only loosely.
Science's unity is the mutually perfecting connection of partial habits along and across chains of demonstration.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e1835.summary: Heading of the second article: what to hold about the numerical unity of a scientific habit, set out in three propositions. (Part of the opening text is displaced into the next paragraph in the transcription.)

ol96b1-c13061-d1e1844.summary: First proposition: a science's unity is that of a whole. A habit could be one in four ways: by simplicity (impossible, against Henry), by continuity like whiteness (impossible, since nothing continuous and quantified is in the intellect), by aggregation like grammar, logic and geometry in one soul or stones in a heap (which would require a complete habit per conclusion, refuted), or by totality, as a house is one by one form and a figure from many lines by one resultant form. Science has the last. Second proposition: science is taken properly or loosely. Memory of a science's demonstrations (all of geometry) is science only loosely, being a habit of the whole deduction and not generated by demonstration but identical with it retained. It has the unity of an order and whole, like a speech or syllogism, made of the species of extremes, middle and their joinings retained in the intellect, from which one can recall the demonstration at will. Science properly is the habit of knowing the conclusion's truth from the principle's.
claims: A scientific habit has the unity of a whole, not simplicity, continuity or aggregation.
Retained demonstrations are science only loosely and have the unity of an ordered whole.
Science properly is the habit of knowing conclusions through principles.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e1959.summary: Third proposition: science properly, the habit of all a science's conclusions, has the unity of a whole whose form is the connection of the partial habits. Demonstrations are 'thickened' (Posterior Analytics) lengthwise, one conclusion inferring another (ordered attributes by mediacy to the subject), and widthwise, several attributes concluded through one middle. These connections perfect one another: the second conclusion is known through the first, which is better known once the second is seen to follow; two conclusions from one middle make the middle better known and so each other. All the conclusions form one integral knowable and their habits one total habit. This suffices: it is a formal unity, as a syllogism is one by joining extremes in the middle, and it explains everything said of science, how error about the hundredth conclusion coexists with knowing the first, how science is acquired successively, why there are not as many sciences as conclusions, and why one who knows Physics I is an imperfect physicist. Conclusions illuminate each other, which is why experts judge well even new cases in their field, like a jurist with cases. Specific unity is treated in article 4.
claims: A science's numerical unity is the connection of its partial habits, which mutually perfect one another.
Demonstrations are connected lengthwise (successive conclusions) and widthwise (common middle).
This connective unity is a formal unity sufficient for a science.
It explains successive acquisition, partial error and imperfect possession of a science.

ol96b1-c13061-Dd1e2121.summary: Reviews and rejects the doctors' accounts of theology's unity. Thomas's unity by revealability fails: revelation, like the agent intellect's light, can illuminate many sciences; revealability, a relation, cannot be the same formal object as deity; infused sciences (Solomon) and a common teacher do not unify habits. Unity by the authority from which evidence derives fails, since theology's declarative clarity comes from natural means and presupposes faith's adherence. Unity by the probative middle fails, since quia and propter quid knowledge and natural science's four causes show diverse middles within one habit. Scotus's unity by formal object fails, since no level of generality of a formal character yields the right number of sciences, and powers and habits (sight and common sense, opinion and science) can share objects. The concurrence view fails for the same reasons and because the three factors are causally ordered. Godfrey's two habits make Scripture disordered, reduce theology's unity to binding (Avicenna's Shifa') or extrinsic end, contradict Augustine's 'this science', ignore faith's unity across speculative and moral matter, and rest on the false thesis that theology is simply both practical and speculative.
claims: Revealability does not unify theology.
Theology's unity does not come from divine authority, since its clarity is naturally derived.
Diverse middles can belong to one habit.
Unity of formal character alone cannot ground the unity of a science.
Theology is not two habits, practical and speculative.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e2130.summary: Rubric naming Thomas Aquinas's opinion (Summa theologiae I q. 1 a. 3).

ol96b1-c13061-d1e2135.summary: States Thomas's view: theology is one because it treats everything (angels, humans, God, creatures) insofar as divinely revealable, and since revelation functions as a light, theology is one by unity of light. Supported by the second group of arguments. Auriol replies: divine revelation is to what it reveals as the agent intellect's illumination is to what it illuminates, and things known by the agent intellect's light belong to diverse sciences, so things known by revelation could too.
claims: (Reported) Theology is one because it considers all things as divinely revealable.
Unity of illuminating light does not unify the sciences, as the agent intellect shows.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e2198.summary: Further objection to Thomas: on his view revealability is theology's formal objective reason, but he also holds that its subject is God under the formality of deity. Revealability is a relation and deity something absolute, so they cannot both be the one formal object. The two claims conflict.
claims: Revealability (a relation) and deity (absolute) cannot both be theology's formal object.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e2249.summary: Further objection: someone could know geometry, physics and ethics as divinely revealed, if God infused them as perhaps he did in Solomon, and he would have several sciences and habits. So revelation does not prevent plurality in theology.
claims: Infused sciences remain distinct despite a common revealed origin.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e2275.summary: Further objection: in revealing theology God acted as principal teacher, and one can acquire several sciences from the same teacher, so theology could be several habits.
claims: A single teacher can teach several sciences.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e2293.summary: Rubric naming the opinion of 'Henricus Anglicus' (Quodlibet I q. 3).

ol96b1-c13061-d1e2298.summary: States the view that light or evidence unifies a habit. Some habits draw evidence from the object (conclusion from principles, principles from terms, attribute from subject) and are distinguished by objects; others, like faith, draw it from a speaker's authority and are unified by it, so faith is one though its contents vary. Theology belongs to the second kind, unified by God's revealing authority. Auriol replies that theology is declarative, not adhesive, and the clarity it gives comes from probable propositions, solved doubts and explained terms, which is natural evidence, not evidence from a speaker's authority.
claims: (Reported) Habits deriving evidence from authority are unified by that authority.
The theological habit's clarity comes from natural means, not from authority.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e2361.summary: Further objection: a habit that presupposes the adherence derived from authority and strives toward fuller evidence does not draw its evidence from authority. Theology presupposes faith's adherence to God's authority and seeks understanding, so it is not unified by authority. (The end is corrupt.)
claims: Theology presupposes faith's adherence and seeks further understanding.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e2390.summary: Rubric for the opinion that theology is one by its middle.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e2398.summary: States the view that a science is one by its probative middle, and theology proves everything by divine authority and first truth, supported by the third group of arguments. Auriol replies that 'quia' and 'propter quid' demonstrations use different middles yet can belong to one habit: the astronomer knows that an eclipse will occur and why (the earth's interposition). That Aristotle calls them different sciences is true of partial sciences, which can still be parts of one habit in the sense explained.
claims: (Reported) Unity of probative middle unifies a science.
Quia and propter quid knowledge of the same conclusion can belong to one habit.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e2455.summary: Further objection: the physicist demonstrates through all four causes (Physics II), which supply middles of different kinds (Posterior Analytics II), so one habit can have diverse middles. Confirmed: Aristotle holds that all kinds of causes can belong to one science, which Averroes says is found only in natural science.
claims: Natural science demonstrates through all four causes.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e2486.summary: Rubric naming Scotus's opinion (Ordinatio prologue q. 3) that theology is one by the formal character of its object.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e2497.summary: States Scotus's view: a science is one by its formal object, and theology's formal object is supremely one, supported by the fourth group of arguments. Auriol objects that unity of formal character is not enough. If it were, the unity would be specific (as many sciences as lowest species), subaltern-generic (as many as subaltern genera), most-generic (only ten sciences, one per category), or that of being (only one science). None works.
claims: (Reported) A science's unity comes from its formal object.
Unity of formal character at any level of generality cannot account for the unity of sciences.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e2545.summary: Further objection: as habits relate to objects, so do powers, and two powers can bear on the same object under the same character (common sense and sight on color; intellect and will on the good), so two habits can as well.
claims: Different powers can share one formal object.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e2567.summary: Further objection: opinion and science are diverse habits yet can concern the same thing under the same character.
claims: Opinion and science can share an object and formal character.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e2577.summary: Rubric for the opinion that theology is one by the concurrence of all factors.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e2588.summary: States the view that formal object, middle and light are all needed for unity, and theology has all three, supported by the fifth group of arguments. Auriol replies that a habit can remain one and uniform with varied middles, as in natural science through all causes and quia/propter quid knowledge of one thing.
claims: (Reported) Unity of science requires unity of object, middle and light together.
One habit can have diverse middles.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e2614.summary: Further objection: among ordered things the first is the cause, and the formal object, middle and light are ordered. Unity of definition and middle comes from the formal object, and evidence and light from the middle. So even if all concur, one has causal priority.
claims: Formal object, middle and light are ordered, with the formal object prior.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e2634.summary: Rubric naming Godfrey of Fontaines' opinion (Quodlibet XIII q. 1) that theology is several habits.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e2641.summary: States Godfrey's view: theology is not simply one, being as perfect about operables as human ethics and about speculables as metaphysics, so it is two habits, practical and speculative, more closely connected than metaphysics and ethics because both are ordered to beatitude as proximate end. Supported by the sixth group of arguments. Auriol calls it very unreasonable: no disorder should be attributed to God or this science, yet with two habits God would have taught it most disorderedly, mixing morals and speculation within small spaces and in nearly every chapter.
claims: (Reported) Theology is two habits, practical and speculative, joined by a common end.
Two habits would make Scripture's teaching disordered.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e2702.summary: Further objection to Godfrey: theology aggregated from two habits would be one only by being bound in one volume, like Avicenna's Shifa' (logic, physics, an abridged Euclid, Almagest, arithmetic, metaphysics and ethics in one book), or by being ordered to one extrinsic end, and then no more one than all sciences (all ordered to beatitude, per Avicenna) or than wool-making and tailoring (ordered to clothes) or masonry and carpentry (ordered to the house).
claims: Unity by binding or by extrinsic end is too weak to make theology one.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e2755.summary: Further objection from Augustine: he speaks of theology as 'this science', not attributing to it all that can be known of human things, and calls theology 'discourse or reason about God' (City of God VIII). With two habits he should have said 'these sciences'.
claims: Augustine treats theology as a single science about God.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e2775.summary: Further objection: faith extends to speculables (God is triune) and operables (simple fornication is mortal sin), all of Scripture, yet is one habit because it adheres to everything for first truth. So theology, treating everything as related to the deity, is one habit.
claims: Faith is one habit covering speculative and moral truths.
Theology is one because it treats everything in relation to the deity.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e2801.summary: Final objection to Godfrey: his position rests on the false premise that theology is simply practical and simply speculative (refuted in the previous question). This ends the review of opinions.
claims: Theology is not simply both practical and speculative.

ol96b1-c13061-Dd1e2813.summary: Auriol's own account of the specific unity of science and of theology. First proposition: every science is specifically one by a single mode of knowing, meaning a uniform way of taking principles (custom, experience, imagination, abstraction), a uniform way of demonstrating, and a uniform stance of the intellect (extended to sense or imagination, reflected on its own acts or on the will's, turned toward pure intelligibles). This is proved from causes, from the intellect, from the formal character of science, by induction over the categories and mathematical sciences, and from Averroes' doctrine that each science has its own logic; conclusions needing another logic belong to another science, as in subalternation. Second proposition: theology is one habit, numerically and specifically, taking as principles whatever supports faith and using them only to declare, connected lengthwise and widthwise; only infallibly true articles can sustain such a declarative habit consistent with all knowledge. The replies apply this: science has parts and the unity of a whole; definitions, middles and principles distinguish sciences only through mode of knowing; a common object or the presence of God does not unify distinct habits; foreign conclusions can be attached to theology as in mixed sciences; and God and creatures fall under one science by attribution.
claims: A science's specific unity comes from its single mode of knowing and proper logic.
Theology is one habit, numerically and specifically.
Theology takes whatever supports faith as principles and uses them only declaratively.
Definitions, middles and principles distinguish sciences only through their mode of knowing.
God and creatures fall under one science by attribution.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e2822.summary: Heading of the fourth article: where the unity of the theological and other habits comes from, according to Auriol.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e2829.summary: Announces two propositions. The first: the unity of every scientific habit comes from one specific mode of knowing, a mode of knowing of the same kind, proved in several ways.
claims: A science's specific unity comes from a single specific mode of knowing.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e2849.summary: First proof, from causes: agents of different kinds produce specifically distinct effects, and principles and demonstrative deduction act as instruments of the agent intellect in producing science (Averroes). Principles differ in kind by how they are known: rational custom (ethics), sensory experience (natural science, medicine), terms grasped imaginatively (mathematics), or abstraction from sense and imagination. Demonstrations also differ in kind: the geometer draws in the dust, the arithmetician computes, mathematicians demonstrate by formal cause, the physicist by all causes, the metaphysician by end and form. So habits of conclusions differ in species with these modes, and a science's unity comes from one mode of knowing.
claims: Principles and demonstrations function as instrumental causes of science.
Sciences take their principles in specifically different ways.
Sciences demonstrate in specifically different ways.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e2924.summary: Second proof, from the intellect: scientific habits perfect the intellect and so are distinguished by its different ways of standing toward objects. It is extended to sensibles (natural science), to spatial imaginables (geometry), to imaginables abstracted from place (arithmetic), turned back on itself toward pure intelligibles (metaphysics), extended to imagination and sense together (optics, astronomy, intermediate sciences), reflected on its own simple and discursive acts (logic, rhetoric, grammar), or on voluntary acts (ethics). Confirmed by Aristotle: things relate to intellect as to abstraction, and there are three real speculative sciences by three modes of abstraction (Metaphysics VI).
claims: Sciences are distinguished by the intellect's different modes of relating to objects.
The three speculative sciences correspond to three modes of abstraction.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e2996.summary: Third proof, from the formal character of science: a habit of the conclusion generated from the habit of principles by necessary demonstrative application. A genus is divided into species by differences that divide its proper formal character, as rational and irrational, which divide knowing, divide animal, while winged and wingless do not. So sciences differ specifically by being generated from principles and demonstrations of different kinds, that is, by different modes of knowing.
claims: Species are constituted by differences that divide the genus's own formal character.
Sciences are specifically distinguished by modes of knowing.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e3038.summary: Fourth proof, by induction: things with a proper mode of knowing need their own science, and things with the same mode belong to one. The ten categories do not make ten sciences: physics covers bodily substance, quantity, sensible qualities, action and passion, place and time as known through principles from sense; metaphysics covers them as known by full abstraction. Yet quantity alone yields four sciences (arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, music) because its species are known in other ways, through principles from imaginatively grasped terms. So sciences are distinguished by modes of knowing. (The text is partly corrupt.)
claims: All ten categories fall under physics as known through sense-derived principles.
Quantity's species ground several mathematical sciences through distinct modes of knowing.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e3116.summary: Fifth proof, from authority. Averroes says each science has its own logic and mode of knowing, besides a logic common to all, and sciences differ by principles and modes of demonstration; Aristotle and Averroes say arts differ by the modes of definition they use; and Physics II seeks the proper mode of demonstrating in natural science. So a science's specific unity comes from one kind of mode of knowing: uniform acceptance of principles, uniform demonstration, and a uniform stance of the intellect in abstraction and extension. Whatever requires a distinct mode has its own science, and everything known in one mode belongs to one science. A science's numerical unity in the soul is one integral cognitive light for truths forming one integral knowable under one specific mode and one proper logic. Conclusions following from others but needing another logic belong to another science, as optics' conclusions from geometry and every subalternate science.
claims: Each science has its own proper logic and mode of knowing.
A science's unity consists in a uniform way of taking principles, demonstrating, and the intellect's stance.
Conclusions requiring a different logic belong to a different science even if derived from another's conclusions.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e3205.summary: Rubric announcing the inference that theology is one habit.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e3212.summary: Second proposition: theology is one habit, numerically and specifically, in a given intellect. It has a uniform mode of taking principles (whatever can help and support faith), one mode of inference (to declare, never to cause adherence), and connection both lengthwise (declaring some articles through others) and widthwise (declaring several articles separately). Objection: the poets' fictions could be declared the same way. Reply: falsehood soon disagrees with truth (Ethics I), so no declarative habit with which all philosophy and experience agree is possible except for the infallibly true articles of faith.
claims: Theology is numerically and specifically one habit.
Theology takes as principles whatever supports faith and uses them only to declare.
Only infallibly true articles can sustain a declarative habit consistent with all philosophy and experience.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e3278.summary: Rubric introducing the replies to the objections.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e3283.summary: Replies to the first argument (every habit is simple): science is not wholly simple but has parts, not quantitative but constitutive of one integral light, as a syllogism has propositions and propositions have terms.
claims: Science has constitutive, non-quantitative parts.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e3301.summary: Replies to the second argument: each part of a scientific habit is simpler than whiteness, but the whole composed of them need not have such unity.
claims: The parts of a science are simple; the whole has the unity of totality.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e3317.summary: Replies to the third argument: habits in the will are also one by totality. Temperance about different foods is not one simple thing, or whoever is temperate in one food would be temperate in all; it is a whole of partial inclinations for different matters.
claims: Volitional virtues like temperance are wholes of partial inclinations.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e3341.summary: Rubric introducing the replies to the second set of arguments.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e3346.summary: Replies to the light argument: the blessed's theology and ours differ not only in light but in mode of knowing, theirs proving a priori and propter quid, ours only declaring from probable reasons and guidance.
claims: The blessed's theology and ours differ in mode of knowing.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e3369.summary: Replies to the habit-of-principles argument: principles vary a science only through different ways of taking them; many principles concur in one science taken in one uniform way.
claims: Principles diversify sciences only through their mode of acceptance.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e3382.summary: Replies to the third light argument: Creator, creature and all physical matters belong to theology insofar as they help the intellect declare believed things.
claims: All matters belong to theology as aids to declaring the faith.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e3402.summary: Rubric introducing the replies to the third set of arguments.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e3407.summary: Replies to the middle argument: definitions and middles distinguish sciences only insofar as they differ in mode of knowing and require a different stance of intellect. Definitions including sensible matter belong to the physicist, whose principles come by extension to sense; those abstracting from it belong to the mathematician, whose principles come by extension to imagination.
claims: Definitions distinguish sciences only through their mode of knowing.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e3436.summary: Replies to the second middle argument: principles lead to knowledge and cause the habit, but they distinguish habits specifically only insofar as they differ in mode of knowing.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e3449.summary: Replies to the round-earth argument, which confirms Auriol's thesis: the proof from parts tending equally to the center belongs to physics because the intellect takes that middle by extension to sensibles (motion), and the proof from the rising and setting of signs belongs to astronomy because it is taken by extension to imagination and sense together.
claims: The round-earth case shows sciences distinguished by mode of knowing, not middle alone.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e3481.summary: Rubric introducing the replies to the fourth set of arguments.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e3486.summary: Replies to the subject-genus argument: a subject genus is one not as one concept (or every concept would have a special science) but by one proper mode of knowing and one proper logic it fixes for knowing truths about itself, as the next question will show.
claims: A subject genus is one through one proper mode of knowing and logic.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e3515.summary: Replies to the argument from powers: two powers, and likewise two habits, can concern one formal object by tending to it in different ways.
claims: Two habits can share one formal object through different modes of tending.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e3526.summary: Replies to the definition argument: unity of definition comes from the formal character of the object, but (in a corrupt text) this does not by itself distinguish sciences.
claims: Unity of definition comes from the formal object.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e3537.summary: Rubric introducing the replies to the fifth set of arguments.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e3542.summary: Replies to the concurrence arguments: even if object, middle and light concur in one whole science, unity comes from the one mode of proceeding. Aristotle's 'one subject genus' (Posterior Analytics I) is what appropriates to itself one mode of knowing, and 'proper definitions' are those with a proper mode of being taken.
claims: The unity of a science comes from its one mode of proceeding.
Aristotle's one subject genus is defined by a proper mode of knowing.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e3569.summary: Rubric introducing the replies to the sixth set of arguments.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e3574.summary: Replies to the 'indivisible object present to each part' argument: if theology were three habits, a common object would not unify them, or opinion and science of one object would be one habit. The rational soul analogy fails, since the soul is present by inhering as form, while God does not inhere in theology as its form.
claims: A common object does not unify distinct habits.
God is not related to theology as a form inhering in it.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e3598.summary: Replies to the 'opinion, faith and declarative habit' argument: theology properly is one declarative habit. As philosophical sciences mix in opinions and other sciences' conclusions (Alhazen's optics includes geometry; Ptolemy teaches chords and arcs in the Almagest, absent from Euclid), so habits of opinion and of metaphysics or physics can be attached to theology for certain conclusions not found elsewhere or discovered by philosophers. They are appropriated to theology because its needs drove the inquiry, as chords and sines are claimed by geometer and astronomer. (The end is cut off.)
claims: Theology properly is one declarative habit.
Other habits can be attached to theology for conclusions its needs prompted, as in the mixed sciences.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e3648.summary: Rubric introducing the replies to the first set of contrary arguments.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e3653.summary: Replies to the arguments that no habit is one: the first and third rightly show that science is not one by simplicity, but they do not disprove unity by totality; the second falsely assumes science is an order of species.
claims: Science is one by totality, not simplicity.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e3673.summary: Rubric introducing the replies to the last arguments.

ol96b1-c13061-d1e3679.summary: Replies to the arguments against theology's unity in particular: even if God and creature shared nothing univocal (perhaps false, as will appear later), they can fall under one scientific act by mutual attribution, which suffices for unity of object (Metaphysics IV). The same answers the second argument.
claims: Unity of attribution suffices for one science of God and creatures.
God and creature may share something univocal (deferred).
